title: Quarter of South Asian Trump Voters Plan Democratic Switch as Discrimination Concerns Rise
excerpt: Indian American Impact poll of 800 voters finds 90 percent have faced or witnessed discrimination, with cost of living and healthcare leading issues ahead of the November 3 midterms.
body:
• Ninety percent of South Asian American registered voters in a new Indian American Impact poll say they have faced discrimination or know someone who has, including 48 percent who experienced it personally.
  • One in four of the community's voters who backed President Donald Trump in 2024 plan to vote Democratic in the November 3 midterms, while 60 percent of likely voters back Democrats for Congress against 22 percent for Republicans.
  • Cost of living (65 percent) and healthcare (53 percent) top the community's issue list, ahead of jobs and wages (33 percent) and education (28 percent).
  • What it means for you: Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. In Michigan, nearly 30,000 registered South Asian voters sat out the 2022 midterms — more than the roughly 19,000 votes that decided the state's 2024 Senate race — so diaspora turnout can decide close races.

Discrimination is a defining concern for Indian American and South Asian American voters heading into the November 3 midterms, according to a nationwide poll released by Indian American Impact, which found nine in ten registered voters have experienced discrimination or know someone who has.

The HIT Strategies survey of 800 South Asian American registered voters found 60 percent of likely voters plan to vote Democratic for Congress, against 22 percent for Republicans and 17 percent undecided. Indian Americans made up 87 percent of respondents, with the rest of Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan, Nepali and other heritage.

"South Asian American voters are paying attention. They want leaders who will bring down the cost of living and protect their healthcare, and they are living through an unprecedented rise in hate."

— Chintan Patel, Executive Director, Indian American Impact

Discrimination Is Near-Universal, Poll Finds

Forty-eight percent of respondents said they had personally faced discrimination. Among those who had, 63 percent most often cited other Americans unfamiliar with South Asian cultures. Eighty-nine percent said what happens to South Asians in the United States affects their personal lives.

https://x.com/anasalhajji/status/2115395181079916857

A February Carnegie Endowment survey found seven in ten Indian Americans disapproved of President Trump's second-term performance, even as only 46 percent identified as Democrats, down from 2020, according to IndiaWest. About one-third supported Trump in 2024.

One in Four Trump Voters Plans to Switch

The sharpest movement is among the community's 2024 Trump voters. Sixty-seven percent of them still plan to vote Republican, but 25 percent plan to vote Democratic. Among 2024 Harris voters, 96 percent plan to support Democrats again.

"There are a large chunk of [Indian American] voters who are, for lack of a better word, having buyers remorse," Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, told local media. "That's something that is building across the community as we're talking about hate and discrimination."

Leaders linked the shift to flashpoints including a post by Texas Railroad Commissioner candidate Bo French about South Asian fans at a University of Texas football game, which Governor Greg Abbott distanced himself from, and an alleged plot to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois. Conservative strategist Anang Mittal said Republican politicians appear to believe there is "no price to be paid" for language treating Indian immigrants as outsiders.

In Texas, Hindu American Foundation board member Rishi Bhutada said some voters plan to vote Democratic straight down the ballot to send Republicans a message. Vasant Bhatt, a 21-year-old who interned on Senator Ted Cruz's 2024 campaign, said he voted early for Democrat James Talarico in Texas's Senate race, citing "xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity," according to GG2.

Cost of Living Leads, and a Movable Middle Remains

On policy, 65 percent of likely voters named the cost of living a top issue and 53 percent named healthcare, followed by jobs and wages at 33 percent and education at 28 percent. Cost of living ranked first across party lines. While 78 percent said their vote can make change, 79 percent said officials quickly lose touch with regular people.

A large bloc is still open to persuasion: pure Independents are 17 percent of registered voters, 72 percent of them undecided, and 16 percent of all voters surveyed have not voted in a general election since 2020.

Impact highlighted two states where those numbers could matter. Michigan has roughly 187,000 South Asian residents, and nearly 30,000 registered South Asian voters there did not vote in 2022 — more than the roughly 19,000 votes that decided the state's 2024 Senate race. In Texas, home to more than 700,000 South Asian residents, nearly 100,000 registered South Asian voters did not vote in 2022.

What to Watch

HIT Strategies surveyed voters September 18 to 26, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.88 points for registered voters. Whether the shift appears in results will be visible first in diaspora-heavy contests in Texas, Michigan, Georgia and Pennsylvania on November 3.
